11800:
A pachyderm is a large, hoofed mammal with an especially thick, tough skin. The word is most commonly used to refer to elephants, but historically it has also been applied to animals like rhinoceroses and hippopotamuses.

When someone says "pachyderm," picture an animal so massive and powerfully built that its skin itself is like a layer of armor — dense, leathery, and tough enough to protect the animal from thorns, the sun, and the rough environments it lives in.

The idea at the heart of this word is thick skin. Not figuratively — literally. These are real, physical animals whose skin is notably, unusually thick compared to most other creatures.

The three animals most associated with this word are:

  • Elephants — by far the most common association. When you hear "pachyderm" in everyday life, it almost always means an elephant.
  • Rhinoceroses — with their armored, wrinkled hide.
  • Hippopotamuses — with their enormous, tough-skinned bodies.

What these animals share is enormous body size, hooves (or hoof-like feet), and that defining thick skin.
Its Place in Science (and Why It Left)

Centuries ago, naturalists — scientists who studied the natural world — grouped all of these thick-skinned animals together into one scientific category called Pachydermata, essentially meaning "the thick-skinned ones." It was a tidy, logical idea at the time.

However, modern science eventually discovered something surprising: these animals are not actually closely related to each other. An elephant, for example, is far more closely related to a hyrax (a small, rodent-like animal) than it is to a rhinoceros. The thick skin was just a coincidence of nature, not a sign of shared ancestry.

Because of this, scientists stopped using "pachyderm" as an official biological term. Today, it is not a scientific classification at all. It belongs to everyday, informal language — not to textbooks or research papers.
How It Is Actually Used Today

In modern usage, "pachyderm" is a slightly formal, old-fashioned, or even playful word for an elephant. You'll often find it in:

  • Literature and journalism, where a writer wants a more sophisticated or unusual word for elephant.
  • Casual conversation, often with a sense of humor or affection.
  • Crossword puzzles and word games, where it appears very frequently.

You would almost never hear a wildlife biologist say it in a serious scientific context. But you might easily hear a tour guide at a zoo say, "Let's go visit the pachyderm house!"

Here are a few sentences showing the word used naturally:

  • "The zoo's oldest pachyderm, a 52-year-old elephant named Raja, celebrated his birthday with a fruit cake."
  • "She watched the great pachyderm lower its trunk into the river and spray water across its back."
  • "In the 19th century, naturalists grouped the rhinoceros and the hippopotamus together with elephants under the label 'pachyderms.'"
  • "The wildlife documentary spent an hour following a herd of pachyderms across the African savanna."
The One Thing to Always Remember

If you ever see or hear the word pachyderm and need to make sense of it instantly, just think: elephant (or, in older/historical contexts, any large thick-skinned mammal like a rhino or hippo). In practically every real-world situation, that one-word mental shortcut will serve you perfectly.
11801: A pacifist is a person who believes that war and violence are never — or almost never — justified, and who is personally committed to resolving conflicts through peaceful means instead.

At the heart of being a pacifist is a deep moral conviction: that no political goal, no matter how important, is worth achieving through killing or large-scale violence. A pacifist looks at war — with all its death, destruction, and suffering — and concludes that it is simply wrong, even when others argue it is "necessary."

This is not timidity or weakness. It is a principled stance. A pacifist is not someone who doesn't care about injustice; in fact, many pacifists care deeply about it. They just insist that the way you fight injustice must itself be non-violent.

A pacifist typically believes one or more of the following:

  • Violence is morally wrong in itself. Taking a human life cannot be justified, regardless of the reason.
  • Violence doesn't solve problems — it creates new ones. Wars breed resentment, destruction, and future conflicts. Peace can only be built through peaceful means.
  • Non-violent alternatives always exist. Negotiation, diplomacy, protest, civil disobedience, economic pressure — these are real tools that can work.

Not all pacifists hold the same position. There is a spectrum:

Absolute pacifists reject violence in every situation, without exception. Even if someone attacks them personally, they would not fight back with lethal force. Even if their country is invaded, they oppose going to war. For them, taking a human life is always wrong, full stop.

Conditional pacifists (sometimes called "pragmatic pacifists") oppose war and large-scale violence but may allow for narrow exceptions — such as defending oneself or others from immediate physical attack. They don't believe war is ever a good solution, but they might not rule it out in the most extreme imaginable scenarios.

The word "pacifist" on its own, without any qualifier, usually refers to someone with a very strong, principled opposition to war — leaning toward the absolute end of this spectrum.

Being a pacifist is not just a private belief — it tends to shape a person's actions in the real world:

  • A pacifist might refuse to serve in the military, even when their country is at war. In many countries, such a person can apply to be a "conscientious objector" — someone who is legally excused from military service because of their moral or religious beliefs.
  • A pacifist might protest against wars being fought by their government.
  • A pacifist might advocate for international institutions like the United Nations or for diplomacy and treaties to prevent conflict.
  • A pacifist might choose non-violent resistance even when facing oppression, rather than taking up arms.

Some of history's most admired figures were pacifists:

  • Mahatma Gandhi led India's independence movement entirely through non-violent means — marches, fasting, civil disobedience — refusing to meet British colonial violence with violence.
  • Martin Luther King Jr. fought for civil rights in America using the same philosophy, inspired directly by Gandhi.
  • Leo Tolstoy, the great Russian novelist, became a committed pacifist in his later life and wrote extensively about why violence was morally indefensible.

These examples show that pacifism is not passive. It often requires enormous personal courage to stand firm against violence without resorting to it yourself.

"Pacifist" does not mean someone who is passive or indifferent. The word can visually suggest "passivity," but that's misleading. Pacifists are often among the most active and courageous people in society — they simply channel that energy into non-violent action.

Pacifism is not the same as being conflict-averse. A pacifist doesn't run from conflict or pretend problems don't exist. They engage with conflict — they just refuse to let it become violent.

Pacifists are not naïve by definition. Critics do argue that pacifism is unrealistic in a dangerous world — that sometimes force is the only thing that stops a dictator or an aggressor. This is a serious, genuine debate. But pacifists have thought-through answers to this challenge: they argue that the long-term costs of war almost always outweigh its supposed benefits, and that humanity has simply not tried hard enough to build truly peaceful systems. Whether you agree or not, this is a reasoned position, not an innocent one.

You will encounter "pacifist" used in a few ways:

  • As a noun describing a person: "She was a lifelong pacifist who marched against every war her country fought."
  • As a label someone applies to themselves with pride: "I'm a pacifist — I don't believe any war can be justified."
  • Sometimes used critically by those who disagree: "The pacifists in parliament are blocking our ability to defend ourselves."
  • In historical or political discussions about war, weapons, and foreign policy.

Pacifism sits within a broader tradition of thought about when — if ever — violence is acceptable. On one side, military thinkers and many governments argue that war is sometimes unavoidable and even morally necessary (this is called "just war theory"). On the other side, pacifists reject this entirely, arguing that the category of "justifiable war" is almost always a rationalization for something unjustifiable.

A pacifist is someone who has drawn a firm line and said: "Whatever the disagreement, however great the injustice, I will not cross into violence to solve it." It is one of the oldest, most consistent, and most seriously-held moral positions in human history.
11802: To pacify means to make someone calm and peaceful, especially when they are angry, upset, or agitated. Think of it as "turning down the heat" on someone's emotions.

When someone is angry, frustrated, or crying, and you do something to calm them down, you are pacifying them.

Examples:

  • A baby is crying loudly. The mother gives the baby a toy. The baby stops crying and settles down. The mother has pacified the baby.
  • A customer is furious about a wrong order at a restaurant. The manager apologizes and offers a free meal. The customer relaxes. The manager pacified the customer.
  • Your little brother is throwing a tantrum because he can't go to the park. You promise to play his favorite game with him instead. He calms down. You pacified him.

Notice the pattern: there is someone in an agitated, upset, or heated emotional state → you do something → they become calm. That action in between is pacifying.
A Very Important Nuance — Pacifying Is Not the Same as Solving

This is the part most learners miss, and it is crucial.

When you pacify someone, you calm their emotional state in the moment. But this does not necessarily mean you have fixed the real, underlying problem.

Think about the restaurant example again. The customer was angry because they got the wrong order. The manager offered a free meal. The customer felt better and stopped being angry. But did the kitchen's mistake get fixed? Not necessarily. The manager pacified the customer — managed the emotional storm — without necessarily solving the root problem.

This is why pacify sometimes carries a slightly negative or dismissive feeling. If someone says, "The government just pacified the protesters with empty promises," it implies the government managed to calm people down on the surface without genuinely addressing what the protesters actually needed or wanted. The word can subtly suggest that the calming was temporary, superficial, or even manipulative.

So the word lives on a spectrum:

  • Sometimes pacifying is genuinely kind and helpful (calming a crying baby).
  • Sometimes it is neutral (a manager handling a difficult customer).
  • Sometimes it is somewhat negative (using tricks or false promises to silence someone's legitimate concerns).

Context tells you which one it is.
The Second Meaning — Bringing Peace to a Place (Not Just a Person)

Pacify can also be used to describe bringing peace or order to a place, particularly a region that is experiencing violence, war, unrest, or rebellion. This is mostly used in military, political, or historical contexts.

Examples:

  • "The general was ordered to pacify the northern territories where rebel groups had been causing unrest."
  • "It took the army several months to pacify the war-torn region."

Here, the target of pacifying is not a single upset person but an entire place full of conflict. The meaning is to suppress the violence and restore order, often by force. Note that this usage almost always carries a negative or at least morally complicated tone, because "pacifying" a region often means using military power to crush resistance — making it peaceful by overpowering those who were fighting.

• Pacify → the base verb (I need to pacify him.)
  • Pacifies → third-person singular present (She always pacifies the crowd easily.)
  • Pacified → past tense and past participle (He was finally pacified after the apology.)
  • Pacifying → present participle (Pacifying an angry crowd is not easy.)
  • Pacification → the noun form (The pacification of the region took years.)
  • Pacifier → a person or thing that pacifies. You may already know this word as the name for the rubber nipple given to babies to suck on — it is literally called a pacifier because its whole purpose is to calm and pacify the baby.
How Pacify Compares to Similar Words

Pacify vs. Calm: These are very close. Calm is broader and more neutral — you can calm a storm, calm your nerves, calm a room. Pacify is slightly more specific: it usually refers to calming someone (or some place) that is actively upset, hostile, or agitated, and it implies a deliberate action or effort to bring about that calm.

Pacify vs. Appease: These are very similar too, and often interchangeable. However, appease leans more toward satisfying someone's demands or desires to gain their goodwill — often by giving them what they want (or something close to it). Pacify focuses more purely on calming the emotional or violent state, regardless of whether demands were met. And "appease" almost always has a negative connotation (suggesting you're giving in too easily), while "pacify" is more neutral.

Pacify vs. Satisfy: Satisfy means to fully meet someone's needs or desires — they get what they actually wanted. Pacify, as we discussed, does not require that. You can pacify someone without satisfying them at all. A distracting toy pacifies a baby who is crying from hunger, but it does not satisfy the hunger.
A Simple Way to Always Remember It

The word pacify is directly related to the word peace. Both come from the same root idea of peace and calm (you can see the connection in words like Pacific Ocean — named for its calm waters — and pacifist — someone who believes in peace over war). So whenever you see or hear pacify, anchor it to the idea of "making peace" — turning something stormy, angry, or violent into something calm and settled.
11803:
A pact is a serious, deliberate agreement between two or more parties — whether individuals, friends, organizations, or entire countries — in which everyone involved mutually commits to doing something, or to not doing something, together.

The most important word here is mutual. A pact is never one-sided. When two people (or two nations) form a pact, every side is making a commitment, not just one. This is what separates a pact from a simple promise, where only one person pledges something to another. A pact is essentially a bundle of interlocking promises, flowing in all directions at once.

Equally important is the weight of a pact. People don't stumble into one accidentally. A pact is entered consciously, deliberately, and with a sense of seriousness. When someone says "we have a pact," the silent understanding is that this is something to be honored — not casually set aside.
Does a Pact Have to Be Written or Legal?

No — and this is a crucial point. A pact does not need to be a formal document, a signed contract, or anything legally binding. In everyday life, pacts are very often informal: two friends looking each other in the eyes, a verbal commitment between siblings, a handshake between partners. The binding force of a pact comes from moral obligation and trust, not necessarily from the law. That said, pacts can absolutely be formal and official — and often are when governments or large organizations are involved.
Where Pacts Show Up in Real Life

Pacts appear in personal relationships. Two friends might make a pact to be completely honest with each other, no matter what. Siblings might make a pact to share the responsibility of caring for aging parents equally. A group going through a hard time together might form a pact to always support one another.

Pacts also appear in business. Two companies might enter a pact not to recruit each other's employees, or to collaborate on a project while agreeing not to leak confidential information to outsiders.

And pacts are perhaps most visible in politics and international relations. Countries sign pacts to govern how they will behave toward one another. A non-aggression pact is an agreement between two countries that they will not attack each other militarily. A defense pact means the countries agree to protect one another if one is attacked by an outside force. A trade pact sets the rules for how goods and services will flow between countries.

One darker and very specific use of the word is a suicide pact — an agreement between two or more people to end their lives together. This is mentioned purely for completeness, since encountering the phrase without context could be jarring and confusing.
How a Pact Differs from Similar Words

Pact vs. Promise: A promise is one-directional — one person commits something to another. A pact is multi-directional — every party commits at the same time. You make a promise to someone; you make a pact with someone.

Pact vs. Agreement: "Agreement" is a broad umbrella covering any situation where people are on the same page. A pact is a specific, intentional, and serious kind of agreement — always centered on a mutual commitment to action or behavior. All pacts are agreements, but not all agreements are pacts.

Pact vs. Deal: A "deal" usually implies exchange — you give me this, I give you that. A pact is less transactional. It's more about a shared commitment, a code of conduct, or a course of action that all parties bind themselves to. Pacts feel more solemn and bond-like than deals.

Pact vs. Treaty: A treaty is the most formal kind of agreement between nations — written, officially signed, and legally binding under international law. "Pact" is sometimes used in international contexts the same way as "treaty," but pact has one important quality that treaty does not: it comfortably describes informal personal agreements between ordinary people. You would never call a handshake agreement between friends a "treaty." You can absolutely call it a "pact."

Pact vs. Contract: A contract is a legally enforceable, usually written agreement — break it, and there are legal consequences. A pact may or may not be written, and may or may not be legally enforceable. People feel bound by a pact through honor, loyalty, and trust — not just legal threat. This moral dimension is part of what gives the word its weight.
How "Pact" Is Typically Used in Language

You make a pact, sign a pact, or enter into a pact. You honor a pact by keeping to what was agreed, or break a pact by going back on it. Breaking a pact is almost always seen as a serious betrayal — not just a minor mistake — whether the pact was personal or political. The word carries that gravity in every context it appears in.

"The two neighboring countries signed a peace pact, agreeing to end decades of hostility."

"As teenagers, the four friends made a pact: no matter where life took them, they would always come through for each other in a crisis."

"She felt crushed when she realized he had broken their pact — it felt like a profound betrayal of trust."

"The rival corporations entered into a pact to pool their research and bring a new technology to market faster."

A pact is a serious, mutual commitment made between two or more parties — personal or political, formal or informal — in which everyone involved binds themselves to the same course of action or conduct, by honor, trust, or law.
11804:
A paddock is a small, enclosed piece of land — fenced in on all sides — that sits next to or near a stable (a building where horses are kept). It is an outdoor space where horses can spend time freely: grazing on grass, stretching their legs, or simply being outdoors in a controlled, safe area.

Think of it this way: a horse spends its nights and rest time inside the stable, but during the day it may be let out into the paddock — its own little private outdoor yard, essentially.

Key characteristics of a paddock in this core sense:

  • It is always enclosed — there is always a fence, wall, or rail around it. This is non-negotiable to the word's meaning. An open field is not a paddock.
  • It is small to medium in size — much smaller than a large farm field or a big open pasture.
  • It is attached to, or very close to, a stable or farm building.
  • It is primarily associated with horses, though sometimes used for other livestock like cattle or sheep.
  • Its purpose is practical: to give animals a safe outdoor space for exercise and grazing.

The paddock is not the same as a stable (which is an indoor building). It is the outdoor extension of that stable — the animal's private outdoor zone.

In the world of horse racing, "paddock" takes on a more specific, well-known meaning: it refers to a special enclosure at a racecourse (the venue where races are held) where horses are brought before each race begins.

Here is what happens in a racing paddock:

  • The racehorses are led into this enclosed area and walked around slowly in a ring or circle.
  • Spectators (the crowd), along with professional punters (people who bet on races), can observe and inspect the horses up close — watching how they move, how calm or nervous they appear, how healthy they look. This helps them decide which horse to bet on.
  • Trainers (the professionals who prepare the horses) and owners gather here to give final instructions to jockeys (the riders).
  • The jockeys mount their horses in the paddock — this is where they physically climb onto the horse and get ready for the race.

So in racing, the paddock is essentially the preparation and display zone — a behind-the-scenes-but-visible stage just before the actual race. After the paddock, the horses head to the starting line.

Perhaps the most widely recognized modern use of the word comes from Formula 1 and other motorsports. Here, the paddock refers to a large, restricted area behind the pit lane at a racing circuit (the track where car races are held).

This is the operational nerve centre of a race weekend. Inside the paddock, you will find:

  • The team garages — the working spaces where mechanics prepare, adjust, and repair the racing cars.
  • Transporters and motorhomes — large vehicles and mobile hospitality units brought by each racing team.
  • Team personnel — engineers, mechanics, strategists, team principals (the bosses), and many other staff members.
  • Media and press — journalists and broadcasters who cover the event.
  • Sponsors and VIPs — important guests and business partners of the teams.
  • Occasionally, fans who have purchased special access passes.

In motorsport, the paddock is not open to the general public without special credentials or passes. It is a private, working environment — the "backstage" of the race. You might hear phrases like "paddock access," "paddock pass," or "sources in the paddock" (meaning people with insider knowledge from within the teams).

The word is so central to motorsport culture that you will frequently hear phrases like "the paddock is buzzing with rumours" or "there is growing tension in the paddock" — here, "the paddock" is used almost as shorthand for the entire community of people involved in that sport at that moment.
The Australian and New Zealand Meaning

In Australian and New Zealand English, the word "paddock" is used far more broadly and casually than anywhere else. In these countries, a paddock simply means any enclosed field — not necessarily one tied to horses.

An Australian or New Zealander might say:

  • "The sheep are in the back paddock."
  • "We drove past a big paddock full of cattle."
  • "The kids are playing in the paddock." (meaning an open grassy field, even a plain field near a house)

In this usage, a paddock is essentially equivalent to what British or American English speakers would call a "field" — any piece of enclosed land, regardless of what it is used for. This broader usage is so common in Australia and New Zealand that a paddock there does not have to be near a stable or have any connection to horses at all.

ContextWhat "paddock" means

The word always carries the idea of an enclosed, defined area — that thread runs through every meaning. Whether it is a small fenced field next to a stable for horses to graze, a dedicated enclosure at a racetrack where horses and jockeys prepare before a race, the backstage operational zone of a Formula 1 event, or simply any fenced field in Australia — the concept of a clearly bounded, purposeful space is always present.

The context will almost always make it obvious which meaning is intended: if someone is talking about horse racing or farms, they mean the first or second sense; if they are discussing Formula 1 or motorsport, they mean the third; if they are in or talking about Australia or New Zealand, they may mean the fourth.
11805: The word paddy has two completely separate meanings that have nothing to do with each other. Context always makes it clear which one is being used.

This is by far the most common and widely used meaning of the word.

What it means

Paddy refers to rice — but specifically rice in its natural, raw, unprocessed state, still wrapped in its outer shell (called a husk). When rice is harvested from the plant, it doesn't look like the clean white grains you cook at home. It still has a tough, brownish-golden covering around each grain. That grain, with the husk still on, is called paddy (or sometimes paddy rice or rough rice).

Once farmers remove the husk, it becomes brown rice. After further processing to strip away more layers, it becomes the familiar white rice people eat. So "paddy" is essentially rice at its most natural stage — straight from the plant, before any processing.

Paddy fields

By natural extension, paddy also refers to the fields where rice is grown. A paddy field (sometimes called a paddy on its own) is a flooded, muddy field in which rice plants grow. Rice needs standing water around its roots for much of its growing period, so these fields are deliberately kept wet or completely submerged in water during the growing season.

Paddy fields are a defining feature of agriculture across South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, and parts of Africa. The terraced, water-filled rice fields you might have seen in pictures from places like Bali, Vietnam, or the Indian countryside — those are paddy fields.

Examples in use:

  • "The farmers harvested thousands of tonnes of paddy this season."
  • "The village was surrounded by green paddy fields as far as the eye could see."
  • "Paddy cultivation requires careful management of water levels throughout the season."

Important distinction

When someone says "paddy" in an agricultural or food context, they almost always mean rice — either the grain in its husk, or the field where it's grown. The two usages are closely connected: paddy (the crop) grows in paddy (the field).
Meaning 2: A fit of anger or temper (informal, British and Irish)

This meaning is entirely unrelated to rice. It is informal and mainly used in British and Irish English.

What it means

A paddy (in this sense) is a sudden burst of bad temper — a childish or irrational fit of anger, frustration, or sulking. It's the kind of rage or tantrum where someone overreacts, storms off, or makes a fuss over something that perhaps doesn't deserve such a strong reaction.

It's often used with the phrases "in a paddy" (meaning currently angry) or "throw a paddy" (meaning to have or perform this tantrum).

Examples in use:

  • "He threw a complete paddy when the restaurant got his order wrong."
  • "Don't get in a paddy over such a small thing."
  • "She stormed off in a paddy after losing the argument."

Register and tone

This is a casual, informal word. You wouldn't use it in a formal letter or serious writing. It's the kind of word someone uses when telling a story about someone overreacting: slightly amused, slightly dismissive of the anger. It often carries a tone suggesting the anger was unnecessary or excessive.
Quick summary of the two meanings

Paddy (meaning 1) — Rice in its unprocessed, husked state; or the flooded field where rice is grown. Used globally, especially in agriculture, food, and geography contexts.

Paddy (meaning 2) — A fit of anger or a childish tantrum. Informal British and Irish English only.

If someone in India, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, or Japan says "paddy," they almost certainly mean rice or rice fields. If someone in Britain or Ireland says "paddy," it could mean either — but outside of agricultural talk, it probably means a bad temper.
11806: A padlock is a portable, detachable lock — meaning it is not built into a door, gate, or any object. You can carry it around, attach it to something to secure it, and remove it whenever you want. This portability is the single most defining quality of a padlock: it belongs to no particular object permanently. You own the padlock, not the gate or the locker.

A padlock has two main visible parts:

  1. The body — This is the solid, chunky main part of the padlock. It is usually shaped like a rectangle or a rounded rectangle, and it houses the internal locking mechanism. It is typically made of metal (often hardened steel or brass), though the outer casing is sometimes covered in rubber or plastic to protect it from weather.
  2. The shackle — This is the curved, U-shaped metal loop that sticks out from the top of the body. It is the part that actually goes through something — a chain link, a metal ring on a gate, the zipper of a bag, the loop of a bicycle rack — and when it clicks shut into the body, it holds everything locked together. The shackle can be short or long, thin or thick, depending on the type of padlock.

When a padlock is open, the shackle is released from the body on one side, allowing you to swing it free and unhook it from whatever it was securing. When it is locked, the shackle is firmly held inside the body by an internal mechanism, so it cannot be pulled free.

A padlock can be opened in one of two main ways:

  • With a key — You insert the correct key into a keyhole on the body, turn it, and the internal mechanism releases the shackle. This is the most traditional type. If you do not have the right key, the padlock will not open.
  • With a combination — Some padlocks have no keyhole at all. Instead, they have a rotating dial or a series of numbered rings. You rotate them to line up the correct sequence of numbers (your secret code), and the shackle releases. These are called combination padlocks. You may have seen them on school lockers.

You use a padlock by passing its shackle through or around something that connects two things you want to keep joined — and then clicking it shut. For example:

  • You loop a chain through a bicycle wheel and around a post, then pass the padlock's shackle through two links of the chain and lock it. Now the chain cannot be removed, and your bicycle cannot be taken.
  • A storage shed might have a metal loop (called a hasp) on the door and frame. You fold the hasp over, insert the padlock's shackle through the holes, and lock it. The door cannot be opened.
  • School or gym lockers often have a small built-in hook where a padlock's shackle hangs, holding the locker shut.

The padlock works as a security link — it is the thing that physically prevents two objects from being separated.
How it differs from other kinds of locks

It helps to know what a padlock is not, so the concept becomes sharper:

  • A door lock (like the knob or deadbolt on a house door) is permanently built into the door. You cannot remove it and take it with you. A padlock, by contrast, is not permanently fixed anywhere.
  • A bolt lock or latch is a mechanism that is part of a door or cabinet and slides into a slot. It has no separate portable component.

What makes a padlock special is that it is self-contained — the entire locking device is in one single portable unit. The shackle and the locking body are always together as one object.

• Keyed padlock — Opens with a key. Very common. Good security.
  • Combination padlock — Opens with a numeric or alphanumeric code. No key to lose. Very common for lockers and low-to-medium security needs.
  • Keyed-alike padlocks — A set of padlocks that all open with the same single key. Convenient when you have multiple locks but want to carry just one key.
  • Hardened padlock — Made with an extra-tough shackle (often hardened steel or boron steel) that is very resistant to bolt cutters. Used where higher security is needed — warehouses, construction sites, etc.
  • Weatherproof padlock — Designed to resist rain, rust, and temperature changes. Used outdoors.
  • Mini/luggage padlock — A very small padlock used on suitcases, bags, or small lockers.
Where you will encounter padlocks in real life

• Bicycle locks and chains
  • Storage units and sheds
  • School and gym lockers
  • Luggage and travel bags
  • Gates, fences, and warehouses
  • Shipping containers
  • Display cases
  • Some cupboards and chests
The core idea, in one sentence

A padlock is a standalone, portable lock with a U-shaped shackle that you thread through two connected objects and click shut, preventing them from being separated — and you open it again with a key or a combination that only you know.
11807: "Padre" is an English word used to refer to a Christian clergyman — someone who is an ordained priest, minister, or chaplain. It has two closely related but distinct uses, and knowing both will give you the complete picture.

"Padre" is used to refer to a Catholic priest, especially in places with Spanish, Italian, or Latin American cultural influence — think Mexico, Spain, Italy, or the American Southwest.

It works both as a title and as a descriptive word. You could address a priest directly by saying "Good morning, Padre," or you could talk about him to someone else: "Go speak to the padre about your troubles."

Think of it as the equivalent of calling a priest "Father" — it's respectful, but warmer and more personal than a formal title. It suggests familiarity and approachability.

While it's most strongly tied to Catholic priests, it's sometimes used loosely for any Christian clergyman, though this is less common.
Use 2: A military or institutional chaplain

This is the more widely recognized meaning in British English and in military contexts around the world.

A chaplain is a clergyman who serves not in a church, but inside a non-religious institution — like the army, navy, air force, a prison, or a hospital — to provide spiritual support, prayer, counseling, and moral comfort to the people there.

In the armed forces, the chaplain is almost universally called "the padre," regardless of whether he is Catholic, Protestant, or Anglican. A soldier who needs to talk through grief, fear, or guilt wouldn't say "I need to see the chaplain." He'd say, "I need to see the padre."

This usage is especially prominent in World War I and World War II literature, films, and memoirs — where the padre is a familiar and deeply human figure moving among the soldiers.

• When used as a direct title or address, it's capitalized: "Thank you, Padre." / "Padre Thomas served in the war."
  • When used descriptively, it's lowercase: "The padre walked through the hospital ward."
  • The plural is simply padres: "Several padres were assigned to the regiment."

What makes "padre" special is its tone. Compared to words like priest, clergyman, or reverend — which can feel clinical or distant — "padre" feels warm, intimate, and human. It suggests that this is someone the people around him trust and feel close to. In a military camp or a difficult situation, calling someone "padre" implies he's not just a religious official; he's a comforting presence.
Important boundary: What "padre" does NOT mean

"Padre" is used only for Christian clergy in English. You would not use it for a rabbi (Jewish), an imam (Muslim), a pundit (Hindu), or any non-Christian religious figure. Applying it to them would be incorrect and out of place.

It is also traditionally a male term — historically, all priests and military chaplains addressed this way were men. While the word itself reflects that tradition, modern usage in some contexts is beginning to shift, though calling a female chaplain "padre" remains uncommon and unusual.
When you'll encounter this word in the real world

• War films, novels, and history books — especially about World War I, World War II, or any military setting. "The padre blessed the troops before battle" is a sentence you'll see often.
  • Stories set in Latin America, Spain, Italy, or the American Southwest — where "padre" refers to the local Catholic priest.
  • Prison dramas or hospital stories — where the chaplain visiting inmates or patients might be called "the padre."
  • Casual or humorous speech — someone might jokingly call any religious person "padre," though this is informal and a bit playful.

Padre = a Christian clergyman, specifically:

  1. A Catholic priest, especially in Spanish or Latin-influenced cultures.
  2. A military or institutional chaplain, serving soldiers, prisoners, or hospital patients.

Both uses share the same core idea: a man of faith who serves people up close, in personal and often difficult moments of life — not from behind a pulpit, but right beside them.
11808: A paean is an enthusiastic, joyful expression of praise — something said, written, sung, or created to celebrate a person, a thing, an idea, or an achievement with great warmth, admiration, and delight.

The single most important thing to understand about a paean is that it is not calm, measured, or lukewarm. Ordinary praise says, "this is good." A paean says, "this is wonderful, and I want the whole world to know it." It carries a sense of celebration, almost like a cheer. There is joy and enthusiasm baked into it — not just approval.

If a critic writes a restrained review calling a novel "quite competent," that is not a paean. But if they write a passionate, glowing piece declaring the novel a masterpiece that moved them deeply and deserves to be read by everyone — that is a paean.
What Form Can a Paean Take?

A paean is flexible. It is not locked to one format. It can be:

  • A speech — "The general's address was a paean to the courage of his soldiers."
  • A piece of writing — "Her essay was a paean to the beauty of the natural world."
  • A song or piece of music — "The final movement of the symphony is a paean to human endurance."
  • A film, poem, or any creative work — "The director's film is a paean to the golden age of Hollywood."

Notice that a paean is often said to be to something or for something. This is the standard phrasing. You write a paean to freedom, to a mentor, to a city, to a lost era.

• "His biography of Mozart reads less like an objective account and more like a paean — the author clearly adores the man."
  • "She stood up at the farewell dinner and delivered a heartfelt paean to her retiring professor."
  • "The new park is a paean to thoughtful urban design — every corner of it has been crafted with love."
  • "The song is a paean to summer — carefree, warm, and impossible not to smile at."
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is important, because several words orbit the same territory.

Praise is the broad, general act of saying something is good. A paean is praise turned all the way up — enthusiastic, celebratory, and heart-on-sleeve.

Tribute is about formally honoring someone's contribution. It tends to be respectful and solemn. A paean has more joy and emotional warmth to it.

Eulogy is praise specifically for someone who has died, delivered at a funeral. A paean has no such restriction — it can be for anyone or anything, living or not, real or abstract.

Ode is a specific type of poem. A paean, by contrast, is not bound to poetry — it can be a speech, an essay, a film, or a song.

Compliment is a small, personal, everyday remark. A paean is bigger — it is an extended, wholehearted celebration, not a passing "nice work."

When someone writes a paean, they are sincerely and enthusiastically praising. But when someone describes another person's writing as "a paean," they may sometimes be raising a gentle eyebrow — suggesting the praise is perhaps a little too one-sided, a little too adoring to be fully objective.

For example: "That profile of the CEO is a paean, not a real journalistic piece." Here, calling it a paean is a mild criticism — it implies the writer got swept away with admiration and lost their balance.

So the word can carry either genuine admiration (when you are the one creating the paean) or a slight note of skepticism (when you are observing someone else's paean from the outside). Context will always make clear which is meant.
A paean is an enthusiastic, joyful, heartfelt expression of praise — in speech, writing, music, or art — celebrating a person, thing, idea, or achievement with great warmth and admiration.
11809:
Paella is a famous Spanish rice dish. It comes from Valencia, a sunny region on the eastern coast of Spain, and it is considered one of Spain's most iconic and beloved foods. Today, it is enjoyed all over the world.

The word "paella" can refer to two closely related things: the dish itself (the food you eat) and the special cooking pan it is made in. In most everyday conversations, when someone says "paella," they almost always mean the food.

Paella is a large, flat, and colorful dish. It has a beautiful golden-yellow color, which comes from saffron — a spice made from the dried threads of a flower. Saffron is one of the most expensive spices in the world, and it is what gives paella its signature look and a subtle, earthy flavor.

The dish is typically cooked and served in a wide, round, shallow metal pan with two handles on the sides — and this pan is also called a "paella." The pan is wide and flat on purpose, because paella rice should spread out in a thin, even layer, not pile up like a mound. This allows the rice to cook properly and develop its most prized feature (more on that below).

Paella is a rice dish. The rice used is short-grain, which means each grain is small and slightly round. This type of rice absorbs liquid and flavor very well without turning mushy.

Beyond rice, paella contains a flavorful broth (sometimes made from meat, seafood, or vegetables), olive oil, garlic, tomatoes, and saffron. The other ingredients vary depending on the type of paella:

Paella Valenciana (the original and most traditional kind) contains chicken, rabbit, green beans, and large white butter beans. This is the "real" paella that people from Valencia will fiercely defend as the authentic version.

Seafood Paella is the type most people outside of Spain are familiar with. It contains ingredients like shrimp, mussels, clams, squid, and sometimes fish. No meat is added.

Mixed Paella combines both meat and seafood — a popular version in restaurants around the world, though traditionalists from Valencia may raise an eyebrow at it.

There are also regional and modern variations that use other proteins like duck, pork ribs, or vegetables only.
The Most Special Thing About Paella: The Socarrat

One of the most important and celebrated things about a well-made paella is something called the socarrat. This is the thin, crispy, slightly caramelized layer of rice that forms at the very bottom of the pan during the final moments of cooking.

A good socarrat is not burnt — it is toasted, nutty, and crunchy. It is considered a sign that the cook has done their job well. People who love paella will often scrape the bottom of the pan specifically to get to this layer. If a paella does not have a socarrat, many consider it incomplete.

Paella is cooked over heat — traditionally over an open wood fire outdoors, which adds a smoky depth of flavor. Today, many people cook it on a gas stove or a special outdoor burner.

The cooking process is done entirely in the pan itself, in stages. First, the meat or seafood is browned in olive oil. Then, vegetables and tomatoes are cooked down. Broth and saffron are added next, and when the liquid is boiling, the rice is spread out evenly across the pan. From that point on, the rice is never stirred. This is crucial. Stirring would make it starchy and sticky, more like risotto. Paella rice must stay separate and loose, each grain soaking up flavor on its own.

Paella is a deeply communal, social dish. In Spain — especially in Valencia — it is a tradition to gather family and friends on Sundays, cook a large paella outdoors, and eat it straight from the pan, each person eating from their own section. It is a meal that brings people together.

In restaurants, it is sometimes served in individual portions, but many places still serve it in the pan at the table for a group to share.

Because paella is famous worldwide, it is often misrepresented. Here are some important clarifications:

  • It is not a quick or casual dish. Making a proper paella takes care, the right ingredients, and attention. A rushed or poorly made paella will not have the right texture or flavor.
  • It should not be mushy or sticky. If the rice is soft and clumped together, that is a sign it was overcooked or stirred too much.
  • It is not the same as Spanish rice or fried rice. Those are entirely different dishes with different methods, textures, and flavors.
  • Adding chorizo is controversial. Many Spaniards, especially those from Valencia, consider adding chorizo (a spiced sausage) to paella a serious mistake and an insult to the dish's tradition — even though you will find it in many international restaurants.

Paella is a wide, flat, saffron-golden rice dish from Valencia, Spain. It is cooked in a special shallow pan of the same name, without stirring, to achieve a crispy rice crust at the bottom called the socarrat. It comes in several varieties — most notably the traditional Valencian version with chicken and rabbit, and the internationally popular seafood version. It is more than just food; it is a cultural ritual of gathering, sharing, and taking pride in something made with care.
